prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: After reading the full first-round exchange I keep B018 as a single-part, two-person prize and I have not changed my preferred configuration. The reasons are scientific and I do not rest them on the five-of-eight count, which Danielsson and Johansson rightly say is not merit. The magic-wavelength lattice is one separable idea: it cancels the light shift of the clock transition while holding many atoms without Doppler or recoil broadening, and it was proposed as a concept before it was realised. The consequence is a measured result, not an inferred one. Independent laboratories reach and compare uncertainty near 1e-18, and at that level a height difference of millimetres becomes a measurable gravitational redshift, which Danielsson points out. Lindroth's point that the many-atom clock exposed new physics, namely collisional and many-body shifts, persuades me that the case is more than instrumental, and I would now state that in my own defence of the prize. Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for taking the clock to record accuracy and many-body-limited operation is a two-name credit that matches the actual steps without an arbitrary cut. The chair's summary records that no member disputes originality, maturity or reproduction, so the open question is weighing, not facts.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which I raised against my own first choice and which Johansson, Mehlig, Lindroth, Olsson and Danielsson all repeat, is that lattice clocks stand on cooling (1997), the comb (2005) and ion control (2012), so a sceptic can read the prize as a refinement of honoured metrology. I think the answer lies in the citation, not in the science, and I accept that a citation worded as 'atomic clocks' generally would fail it. Second, a two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, and neither I nor anyone else has verified the priority sequence between the early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks; my recollection is that Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clock came first and Ye's group followed and then drove performance, but that is recollection and the committee should check it before voting. Third, the redefinition of the second is still pending. I now think that argues for neither waiting nor hurrying: the discovery is complete without the redefinition. Finally, a committee that gives more weight to a new messenger than to a precision advance could reasonably prefer B007, and I cannot say that view is wrong, only that the attribution problems there are larger.

responses.point: Pearce keeps IceCube (B007) first, calls an improvement in clock accuracy a gain of degree, wants the committee to say why it should outrank a discovery that created a new field, and agrees the citation should rest on the diffuse flux and not on TXS 0506+056.
responses.response: I accept that discovery character is the real disagreement between us and I will not treat a gain in accuracy as automatically a discovery. My answer is that the lattice clock is not only a gain of degree. The magic-wavelength condition is a qualitative change in what can be done, and at 1e-18 it turns millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, constants and ultralight-field searches into measurements, which Danielsson and Lindroth both stress. Where I do concede ground is that IceCube opened a window, and I would not call a prize for it a mistake. The decisive problem remains the credit. You propose Halzen and Karle, the nomination lists Yoshida, and the discovery was made by a collaboration of hundreds on AMANDA foundations. You did not say in round 1 what separates Karle from Yoshida, and I would still like that answer. If the committee can write a defensible two-name credit, I would move B007 above B032 as my second choice, but I would not move it above B018, where the credit does not need such a defence.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B018 but argues the citation should be written around the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom clock so that it does not repeat 2005, and that the clocks exposed collisional and many-body physics, making my 'measurement-limited' framing too instrumental.
responses.response: I accept both points and I change my wording as a result. The citation I propose now names the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly and does not use a general 'optical clocks' phrase, which also keeps the claim distinct from the comb prize. Your many-body argument is the best reply to the charge that this is metrology only: spin-exchange and collisional shifts in a dense lattice, and the work to control them, are physics learned from the clock and not just engineering. I would only add that Ye's group's role in reaching the many-body-limited regime is exactly why Ye is credited next to Katori, so the point supports the two-name configuration. I do not think we need a sentence about 2005 and 1997 in the citation itself; a citation is better short, and the earlier prizes can be addressed in the committee's background text.

responses.point: Johansson keeps Cirac and Zoller (B032) first, argues that the 2012 prize recognised experiments and not the proposals, and says four first places for B018 do not settle whether it is distinct from the comb and cooling prizes.
responses.response: I agree that four first places do not settle anything, and I have tried to argue from the lattice idea instead. On B032 you answered my round-1 worry partly: the proposals told experimentalists what to build, and 2012 recognised the control of single quantum systems and not the blueprint. That is a fair distinction and I now find a theory-only prize more coherent than I did. What stays with me is the B015 overlap you raise yourself. If Cirac and Zoller are honoured for B032, Bloch and Greiner are left with a weaker claim to B015, and a three-person limit makes any combined configuration awkward. For B018 the comparison with your concern is this: cooling and the comb are tools used by the lattice clock, not the same invention. The magic-wavelength lattice is not contained in either. That is why I place B018 above B032, while keeping B032 as my second alternative because its credit is as clean as the clock's.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps fluctuation theorems (B002) first, does not consider lattice clocks a stronger conceptual discovery, and says magic-wavelength trapping builds on cooling and combs, so the case rests on precision and uses, not a new concept.
responses.response: I take your objection seriously and I partly agree: the sharpest case for B018 is the precision and what it makes measurable. I do not agree that there is no new concept, because the magic-wavelength lattice is a concept, and it was published as one before the clock was operated. On B002, I think the conceptual quality is high, and I do not question the experimental tests in tweezers and single-molecule work. The difficulty remains that the credit is for a family of exact relations. You propose Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert and call Crooks an awkward omission. I would like you to say which single result the citation would name, and who of Evans, Jarzynski and Seifert you would give up if a fourth person had to be added or if the committee judged the steady-state priority contested. Until that is answered I cannot put B002 above a configuration whose two names are agreed by every member who ranked it.

responses.point: Danielsson agrees on maturity and attribution but cautions that a clean two-name list does not itself make B018 scientifically superior to B032, adds that 1e-18 clock comparison makes gravitational redshift over millimetres a measurement, and says the citation should not imply that Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley did not matter.
responses.response: You are right that clean attribution is not a sufficient argument, since B032 also has two clean names. I do not use it as one. My ordering of B018 over B032 rests on the fact that B018 is a measured result with independent comparisons across laboratories, while B032 is a set of proposals whose payoff in scalable quantum computing is not finished. I take your redshift point as the best statement of why this is new capability and not incremental accuracy. On the omitted names, I agree and would put it in the committee's background text, not the citation: the citation should state what Katori and Ye did and not claim the field began with them. I also would not call the clocks proven without noting that I have not verified the early priority sequence either.

uncertainties: The priority between the earliest lattice-clock proposals and the first operating clocks, and the exact roles of Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and others, rest on my own recollection and have not been verified by any member.

Whether the committee, on reflection, regards the lattice step as distinct from the comb and ion-control prizes; I think it is, but the support depends on a judgement about discovery character that members clearly weigh differently.
Whether a defensible two- or three-name IceCube credit exists; if it does, B007 is a stronger competitor than I scored it, and Pearce has not yet answered the Karle versus Yoshida question.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should influence timing; I believe it should not, but this is a judgement and not a verified fact.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented connection to Katori or Ye. A distant link on the record is a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, and Hall is not a credited name for B018. I take part in WACQT management and have worked in quantum information at Lund, so I would stay out of any deciding discussion on circuit QED (B008). No specific conflict is apparent for B018, B007 or B032 from my profile, and the round-1 exchange has not changed that.
